In this framework, higher (i.e., positive) ARS values shift responses toward the right end of the scale, whereas lower (i.e., negative) values shift them toward the left end. To capture this effect, we introduce a person-specific parameter 𝜂 𝑖 ARS , yielding the following equations for the shape parameters of the beta distribution:

Here, 𝑥 𝑗 is an indicator of item direction, taking values of -1 for reverse-scored items and 1 for regular items. This specification is essential for disentangling ARS from the substantive traits. The model assumes that items are coded such that higher observed responses correspond to higher levels of the latent trait. For regular items (𝑥 𝑗 = 1), a positive 𝜂 𝑖 ARS increases the expected response, similar to the effect of a higher latent trait value. For reversescored items (𝑥 𝑗 = -1), a positive 𝜂 𝑖 ARS decreases the expected response, whereas the substantive trait 𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 continues to increase it. This opposing effect across item types enables identification of ARS separately from the latent trait.

Combined Model (BIRM-RS)

Combining the extensions for ERS/MRS and ARS, the final formulation of our extended BIRM-RS model is expressed as:

This formulation encodes a theoretical assumption through the placement of parentheses:

The ARS term 𝜂 𝑖 ARS is included within the scaling by ERS. Conceptually, this implies that the response shift associated with ARS is modulated by the individual's level of ERS, such that ARS effects may be amplified or attenuated depending on the strength of extreme responding.

A graphical illustration of all model parameters is provided in Figure for acquiescent response style (ARS). The study followed current recommendations for simulation studies in psychological research (Siepe et al., 2024) and was preregistered on the

OSF (see Open Practices Statement section).

We varied several factors that could potentially influence model performance. The first set of factors included sample size, the number of items per latent trait, and the number of reverse-scored items. The second set of factors concerned the characteristics of the response styles parameters, specifically their variances and the priors used for their estimation. Given the limited availability of empirical evidence on these parameters, we examined a range of plausible values.

Data Generation

Data were generated according to the BIRM-RS model specified in Equation 5 and (3) to avoid computational difficulties associated with higher-dimensional trait spaces.

For the item parameters, difficulty values (𝛿 𝑗 ) were drawn from a uniform distribution 𝒰(-3,3) to reflect realistic variability, in contrast to the evenly spaced values used in earlier simulation studies (Noel & Dauvier, 2007). Item dispersion (𝜏 𝑗 ) was sampled from 𝒰(0,3), following Noel and Dauvier (2007), thereby covering a wide range of dispersion levels.

The item direction indicator (𝑥 𝑗 ) was fixed at either -1 for reverse-scored items and 1 for regular items, with the proportion of reverse-scored items varying across simulation conditions.

For the person parameters, the two latent traits (𝜃 𝑖1 and 𝜃 𝑖2 ) were drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with variances fixed to 1, as in Noel and Dauvier (2007). The covariance between the two traits was set to 0.2, representing a small positive correlation (also .2) that reflects realistic situations in which latent traits are not fully independent. The covariance between each latent trait and ERS was defined as 0.1 ⋅ 𝜎 ERS , resulting in correlations of approximately .1. This is consistent with findings from Likert-scale research, where small but non-negligible correlations between substantive traits and response styles have been observed (Pokropek et al., 2023).

The variances of ERS (𝜎 ERS 2 ) and ARS (𝜎 ARS 2 ) were systematically varied across simulation conditions to assess their impact on parameter recovery. The ARS parameter 𝜂 𝑖 ARS was drawn independently from 𝒩(0, 𝜎 ARS 2 ), reflecting the assumption that ARS is independent of the substantive traits. Conceptually, ARS captures a general tendency to agree with items regardless of their content; thus, any association between this tendency and the substantive traits should, in theory, already be captured by the traits themselves. Consistent with this assumption, the correlation between ERS and ARS was fixed to zero. This choice also keeps the covariance structure of the data-generating model tractable, as allowing ARS to covary with the substantive traits and with ERS would have added further factors to an already extensive simulation design.

Independence of ARS and the substantive traits should therefore be understood as a simplifying assumption about the data-generating process rather than as a restriction of the model: although the prior on 𝜂 𝑖 ARS implies zero covariance with the substantive traits at the population level, the person-level estimates are not constrained to be uncorrelated, so associations between ARS and the substantive traits can still emerge if the data support them.

The distributions of the person parameters are defined as follows: (

For each person-item pair, the shape parameters of the beta distribution were computed according to the BIRM-RS model (Equation 5), and responses were then drawn as 𝑦 𝑖𝑗 ∼ Beta(𝑚 𝑖𝑗 , 𝑛 𝑖𝑗 ). To prevent numerical instability, responses were truncated to the interval [0.0001, 0.9999], as recommended by Noel and Dauvier (2007).

Simulation Design

The simulation design systematically varied several factors to evaluate their effects on the recovery of person parameters. These factors can be grouped into general factors and response style specific factors, resulting in 61 unique simulation conditions.

General Factors

Sample size: Because larger samples typically improve parameter recovery, we included two levels: 300 and 600 participants. Both values reflect realistic sample sizes in applied research contexts.

Number of items per substantive trait:

We varied the number of items per substantive trait, selecting either 6 or 12 items (i.e., 12 or 24 items in total for the two traits). This range represents typical scale lengths in psychological measurement and should influence parameter recovery, especially for person parameters, as more items provide more information per respondent.

Number of reverse-scored items:

The number of reverse-scored items determines how well the model can disentangle ARS from the substantive traits. To represent the allocation of reverse-scored items across the two latent traits, we use the notation A|B, where A denotes the number of reverse-scored items for the first trait and B for the second trait. For the 6-item-pertrait conditions, the configurations 0|3 and 3|3 were used (i.e., 3 or 6 reverse-scored items in total). For the 12-item-per-trait conditions, the configurations 0|3, 3|3, and 6|6 were used (i.e., 3, 6, or 12 reverse-scored items in total). Additionally, we included one condition to examine whether the model can recover parameters in the absence of reverse-scored items. This condition tested whether ARS can be distinguished from the substantive traits when item direction does not vary. We expected that ARS and the substantive traits would not be separable in this condition.

To facilitate model estimation in this scenario, the remaining design factors were set to values expected to be most favorable for parameter recovery (i.e., 12 items per trait and larger response style variances, etc.).

Response Style Specific Factors

Variances of the response style parameters: Because empirical benchmarks for response style variances in VAS data are currently lacking, we based our choices on theoretical considerations. The substantive trait variance was fixed to 1, serving as a natural reference point.

Response style variances were assumed to be smaller in magnitude. Moreover, because the ERS/MRS parameter (𝜂 𝑖 ERS ) is exponentiated in the model, even small variances can produce substantial effects on the response distributions. Accordingly, we selected three levels of response style variances representing small to moderate variability: 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5.

Prior for the ARS parameter: Pilot simulations indicated that a narrower prior improved parameter recovery. Therefore, we compared a standard normal prior (𝜎 = 1) with a narrower prior (𝜎 = 0.9) for 𝜂 𝑖 ARS . Both priors remain considerably wider than the target variances for ARS and thus should not unduly constrain the estimates.

The full simulation design is summarized in Table 1.

Number of Simulation Replications

The number of simulation replications was determined such that the Monte Carlo Standard Error (MCSE) of the person-parameter performance measures remained below 0.01.

The MCSE quantifies the uncertainty in estimated performance metrics that arises from a finite number of replications; lower MCSE values indicate more precise estimates:

Here, 𝑀 (𝑟) denotes the performance measure computed in replication 𝑟, SD(⋅) is the standard deviation across replications, and 𝑅 is the total number of replications.

To determine an adequate number of replications, we conducted a pilot simulation under challenging conditions, using a sample size of 𝑛 = 300, six items per substantive trait, and varying combinations of reverse-scored items and response style variances, with 10 replications per setup. The largest observed standard deviation across performance measures was 0.063 for the correlation between true and estimated values of one of the latent traits, corresponding to an MCSE of approximately 0.02. Based on this result, we expected that at least 40 replications would be required to achieve an MCSE below 0.01. To ensure sufficient precision, we opted for 50 replications per condition. We further planned to increase the number of replications in steps of 10 if the final MCSE values exceeded the 0.01 threshold.

Priors

We used weakly informative priors to promote computational efficiency while allowing the data to drive parameter estimation. For the substantive traits and the ERS parameter, we specified a multivariate normal prior:

The covariance matrix Σ was estimated using an LKJ(2) prior for the correlation matrix and half-normal priors for the standard deviations. This prior mildly favors correlations near zero, which is consistent with previous empirical findings, while still allowing larger correlations if supported by the data. This regularization enhances computational efficiency without overly constraining the model.

For the ARS parameter, we used normal priors centered at 0 with two alternative standard deviations, where 𝜎 ARS was set to either 1 or 0.9.

Unlike the substantive traits and ERS, which share a multivariate prior, 𝜂 𝑖 ARS is assigned an independent prior. This specification reflects the conceptualization of ARS as a content-independent response tendency and implies zero covariance with the substantive traits at the population level. It does not, however, force the person-level estimates to be uncorrelated: associations between ARS and the substantive traits can emerge if they are present in the data, although they will tend to be shrunk toward zero.

For the item parameters, item difficulty parameters were assigned normal priors centered at 0 with a standard deviation of 3, 𝛿 𝑗 ∼ 𝒩(0,3). Item dispersion parameters were constrained to a lower bound of 0.1 and assigned truncated normal priors with a location of 1 and a scale of 2, 𝜏 𝑗 ∼ 𝒩 [0.1,∞) (1,2). All priors were intentionally set to be wider than the corresponding datagenerating distributions, ensuring that they do not exert undue influence on parameter estimation.

Model Estimation and Analysis

Estimation

After data generation, each dataset was analyzed using the BIRM-RS model as specified in Equation 5, estimating the two latent traits (𝜃 𝑖1 , 𝜃 𝑖2 ), the response style parameters (𝜂 𝑖 ERS , 𝜂 𝑖 ARS ), and the item parameters (𝛿 𝑗 , 𝜏 𝑗 ). Parameter estimation was carried out via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling implemented in Stan (Stan Development Team, 2024), accessed through the CmdStanR interface (Gabry et al., 2025) in R (R Core Team, 2024). For each model, we ran two MCMC chains with 2,000 warm-up iterations and 3,000 post-warm-up iterations per chain; as identified in pilot simulations, these settings were expected to ensure stable sampling and convergence.

Additionally, we truncated the shape parameters 𝑚 𝑖𝑗 and 𝑛 𝑖𝑗 in the Stan model to the interval [exp(-7), exp(7)], corresponding to values between approximately 0.001 and 1,096.63.2 This truncation substantially improved numerical stability and reduced sampling time without substantially affecting the likelihood or posterior estimates.

Extracted Quantities and Diagnostics

From the resulting posterior distributions, we extracted several quantities to evaluate the model. First, we obtained the person parameters: the two latent traits (𝜃 𝑖1 and 𝜃 𝑖2 ), the ERS (𝜂 𝑖 ERS ), and the ARS (𝜂 𝑖 ARS ). Second, we extracted the item parameters, specifically item difficulty (𝛿 𝑗 ) and dispersion (𝜏 𝑗 ). Finally, we recorded standard MCMC diagnostics, including the potential scale reduction factor (𝑅 ̂) and the effective sample size (ESS), to assess convergence and sampling efficiency.

2 This truncation is used solely to improve numerical stability during MCMC sampling and is unrelated to the treatment of responses at the scale boundaries, which is handled separately by rescaling responses prior to estimation. Without these bounds, the sampler can occasionally explore extremely large or small values of the beta shape parameters, for which numerical evaluation of the beta density becomes unstable while the data provide little information to distinguish among increasingly extreme parameter values. The bounds therefore prevent numerical problems in poorly identified extreme regions of the parameter space rather than imposing a substantively meaningful restriction. They are wide relative to the parameter values encountered in practice: in the empirical application, no posterior draw approached either bound.

Performance Measures for Parameter Recovery

We used several metrics to evaluate the recovery of person and item parameters. Each

parameters ranged from <0.0001 to 0.0104. The maximum value slightly exceeded the predefined threshold of 0.01. 4 MCSEs for the item parameters ranged from <0.0001 to 0.0135.

Overall, the factors with the strongest influence on person-parameter recovery were the number of items, the number of reverse-scored items, and the response style variances. Sample size also had a positive, but comparatively smaller, effect. Parameter recovery was slightly better for the ARS prior with a standard deviation of 0.9 compared to 1.0. Results for the 𝜎 = 1.0 prior are reported in the supplementary materials.

A brief summary of item parameter recovery is presented in Table 2; further details are available in the supplementary materials. Across conditions, the range of performance measures indicated that recovery was good even under the least favorable conditions. One consistent pattern was a tendency for the dispersion parameter (𝜏 𝑗 ) to be slightly overestimated, particularly in conditions with high response style variances.

As expected, the condition without reverse-scored items yielded the weakest recovery for the substantive traits and ARS. In this condition, the correlations between true and estimated values were .73 for both substantive traits, and .65 for ARS.

Recovery of Person Parameters

Correlations (Figure 2), RMSEs (Figure 3) and absolute biases (Figure 4) indicate that the substantive traits were well recovered across conditions, particularly with more items in total and a greater number of reverse-scored items. As expected, recovery was weaker for traits without reverse-scored items. ARS recovery followed a similar pattern, showing strong dependence on both the total number of items and the number of reverse-scored items. ERS recovery was more robust, showing good performance across all conditions, with performance further improving as the number of items increased. For both response style parameters, recovery improved with increasing response style variances. Under these conditions, the negative effects of having fewer reverse-scored items on ARS recovery were partially mitigated. For instance, the correlation between the true and estimated ARS values was 𝑟 = .87 in the condition with a sample size of 300, twelve items per substantive trait, no reverse-scored items for the first trait, and response style variances of 0.5. Increasing the sample size improved recovery for all parameters, although the effect was relatively small. RMSEs were higher in conditions with larger response style variances, particularly for the response style parameters. This pattern arises because RMSE is variance dependent and therefore does not necessarily indicate poorer recovery performance. A similar pattern emerged for the mean absolute biases.

Estimation biases are shown in Figure 5. ARS was neither systematically overestimated nor underestimated across conditions. In contrast, the substantive traits were slightly underestimated overall, and ERS showed the largest degree of underestimation across all conditions. This primarily occurred for individuals with high positive ERS values, suggesting that the lower estimated ERS values were still sufficient to reproduce extreme observed responses. Consistent with this interpretation, bias was reduced in conditions with lower response style variances of 0.1, where extreme ERS values were less pronounced.

Variance and Correlation Recovery

Variance estimates for the person parameters are shown in Figure 6. Overall, a greater number of (reverse-scored) items led to improved variance recovery. Across conditions, the variance of ARS was slightly overestimated, whereas the variance of ERS was consistently underestimated. The latter pattern aligns with the bias results and the finding that high ERS values tended to be underestimated. For ARS, the overestimation was small but consistent across conditions.

The correlation between the two substantive traits (𝜌 = .20) was generally well recovered across conditions, ranging from .16 to .27. The only exception was the condition without any reverse-scored items for either trait (r = -.73). The correlations between the substantive traits and ERS (𝜌 = .10) ranged from .09 to .19 for the first trait, and from .08 to .15 for the second trait. Especially for the first trait, correlations were overestimated in conditions with fewer reverse-scored items and fewer items overall. The correlations between the substantive traits and ARS (𝜌 = 0) were also generally well recovered, ranging from -.003 to .16 for the first trait, and from -.02 to .07 for the second trait. These ranges exclude the condition without reverse-scored items, in which the correlations were substantially overestimated (r = .32 for the first trait and r = .32 for the second trait). Overall, correlation recovery improved with increasing numbers of items and reverse-scored items. Differences between the two latent traits can be attributed to the different numbers of reverse-scored items in some conditions.

Summary of Results

In summary, we identified the conditions under which the BIRM-RS model recovered parameters most accurately. The number of items per substantive trait and the number of reversescored items emerged as the most influential design factors, with the latter being critical for disentangling ARS from the substantive traits. In addition, higher response style variances improved the recovery of response style parameters. Taken together, these findings indicate that the BIRM-RS recovers its own parameters well when sufficient item information is available, particularly in terms of scale length and variation in item direction.

Additional Simulation With a Single Substantive Trait

Because disentangling response styles from substantive traits may be more difficult when only a single trait is measured, we conducted an additional simulation with one substantive trait.

We varied sample size (300, 600), the total number of items (6, 12, 18, 24), the number of reverse-scored items (3 up to half of the items), and the response style variances (0.1, 0.3, 0.5), resulting in 60 conditions. Conditions without reverse-scored items were not included because, with only one substantive trait and no variation in item direction, ARS cannot be separately identified from the substantive trait. All other specifications followed those of the main simulation, with the ARS prior set to 0.9.

Recovery depended primarily on the total number of (reverse-scored) items; measuring only a single substantive trait did not in itself impair recovery. With 24 items, 12 of which were reverse-scored, correlations between true and estimated values were .98 for the substantive trait, .91 for ERS, and .82 for ARS at the lowest response style variance. These values closely matched those in the corresponding condition of the main simulation with two substantive traits and the same total number of items. Recovery was weakest with 6 items and 3 reverse-scored items (.91, .67, and .59, respectively). The remaining patterns replicated those of the main simulation: recovery improved with higher response style variances, sample size had little effect, and ERS was again slightly underestimated. Detailed results are reported in the supplementary materials.

Empirical Illustration

To further evaluate the BIRM-RS model, we applied it to self-report data from Kuhlmann et al. (2017). In that study, VAS were used to assess 26 items across three constructs: conscientiousness, excitement seeking, and narcissism. Conscientiousness was assessed with the German NEO-FFI subscale (Borkenau & Ostendorf, 1993), comprising 12 items, including four reverse-scored items. Excitement seeking was measured using the corresponding subscale of the German NEO-PI-R (Ostendorf & Angleitner, 2004), consisting of eight items, including two reverse-scored items. Narcissism was measured using the six-item short version of the German NARQ (Back et al., 2013), which contained no reverse-scored items. Because ARS is modeled as trait-invariant, its estimation can still benefit from reverse-scored items measuring the other two constructs; we return to this issue below (see Post-hoc Simulation section). The dataset included responses from 608 participants (see Kuhlmann et al., 2017).

Our goal was to compare the BIRM-RS model, which incorporates response styles, with model variants that do not include response style parameters, in order to evaluate whether accounting for response styles improves model fit. We fitted four models to the data: (1) the full BIRM-RS including both ERS and ARS (Equation 5), (2) the BIRM-RS with only ERS (BIRM-ERS, Equation 3), (3) the BIRM-RS with only ARS (BIRM-ARS, Equation 4), and (4) the original BIRM without response style parameters (Equation 1). Prior specifications and model assumptions were identical to those used in the simulation study, with the ARS prior standard deviation set to 0.9.

Model fit was evaluated using the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) and the leave-one-out information criterion (LOOIC) (Gelman et al., 2014; Vehtari et al., 2017; Watanabe, 2010). Both indices estimate out-of-sample predictive accuracy while penalizing model complexity, with lower values indicating better fit.

Results

All models converged successfully, with 𝑅 ̂ values below 1.01. Model fit indices are reported in Table 3. The full BIRM-RS model, including both ERS and ARS, showed the best fit according to both WAIC and LOOIC, whereas the original BIRM without response style parameters exhibited the poorest fit. The intermediate models (BIRM-ERS and BIRM-ARS) showed similar performance. Overall, these results indicate that accounting for both response styles improves model fit to the empirical data, supporting the utility of the BIRM-RS for analyzing VAS responses.

Parameter estimates from the BIRM-RS model indicated that the variances of the response style parameters were similar in magnitude to those used in the simulation conditions with the lowest response style variance levels (𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐸𝑅𝑆 = 0.09; 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐴𝑅𝑆 = 0.15). In contrast, the variances of the substantive traits were substantially lower than 1 (𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑢𝑠𝑛𝑒𝑠𝑠 = 0.42; 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐸𝑥𝑐𝑖𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑆𝑒𝑒𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔 = 0.59; 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝑁𝑎𝑟𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑠𝑚 = 0.55). Small correlations were observed between ERS and the substantive traits (𝐶𝑜𝑟 𝐸𝑅𝑆,𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑢𝑠𝑛𝑒𝑠𝑠 = .16; 𝐶𝑜𝑟 𝐸𝑅𝑆,𝐸𝑥𝑐𝑖𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑆𝑒𝑒𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔 = -.07; 𝐶𝑜𝑟 𝐸𝑅𝑆,𝑁𝑎𝑟𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑠𝑚 = -.05). Posterior correlations between ARS and the substantive traits were negligible as well (-.04, -.03, and -.06), consistent with the assumption of independence adopted in the simulation study, although the model would have allowed nonzero correlations between the person-level estimates to emerge. To examine whether the BIRM-RS performs adequately under these empirical conditions, we conducted an additional post-hoc simulation study.

Sensitivity to Boundary Responses

Because the BIRM assigns zero density to the boundary values 0 and 1, responses were rescaled to the interval [0.0001, 0.9999] prior to estimation. In the present data, boundary responses were not rare (4.89% at 0, 5.93% at 1). Because such rescaling is not equivalent to explicitly modeling boundary inflation (Molenaar et al., 2022), we examined whether our substantive conclusions are sensitive to this modeling choice by additionally fitting the zero-and one-inflated BIRM (Molenaar et al., 2022) to the same data. As model fit indices are not directly comparable across these specifications, 5 we instead compared trait variances, trait intercorrelations, person parameter estimates, and item parameters. We also included the BIRM without response style parameters or boundary inflation, allowing us to distinguish differences attributable to the treatment of boundary responses from those attributable to the inclusion of response styles.

The overall pattern of results was unaffected by the treatment of boundary responses. All three trait intercorrelations had the same sign across models, with the correlation between excitement seeking and narcissism clearly the largest in each, item difficulties were virtually indistinguishable (𝑟 = .998), and person parameter estimates of the BIRM-RS and the zero-and one-inflated BIRM correlated between .82 and .91 across the three traits. The main difference concerned the scaling of the latent variances: estimated trait variances were consistently lower under the inflated specification, by approximately one third for two traits and by roughly two 5 WAIC and LOOIC are not directly comparable here because the models are fitted to slightly different data and boundary responses contribute a beta density in the rescaled specification but a probability mass in the inflated specification.

Consequently, the pointwise predictive densities are not on a common scale. thirds for the scale on which boundary responses accumulated at both ends.foot_1 This pattern is consistent with the fact that, under an open-interval likelihood, boundary responses must be accommodated through the beta density itself and are therefore partly attributed to latent variance and to extreme responding. A scatterplot matrix comparing person parameter estimates of the three models (see supplementary materials) indicates that the treatment of boundary responses primarily affected the scale of the person parameter estimates rather than their relative order. Estimates of the BIRM with and without boundary inflation correlated between .89 and .95, with regression slopes ranging from .54 to .81. Including response style parameters changed the estimates of individual respondents to a similar extent (BIRM-RS vs. BIRM without response style parameters: 𝑟 = .87 to .97) but not their scale (slopes of .94 to 1.00). Deviations from these relations were larger for respondents with many boundary responses. The substantive conclusions drawn from the BIRM-RS thus appear robust to the treatment of boundary responses, whereas the absolute magnitude of the estimated latent variances should be interpreted with caution when boundary responses are frequent.

Comparison With Existing Response Style Models for VAS

To relate our model to existing approaches, we additionally fitted the CRM-based extension for ERS/MRS (Huang, 2025) and the beta-based extension for ERS/MRS (Jiang et al., 2025) to the same data. The corresponding ARS extension of the CRM did not converge for these data under either a centered or a non-centered parameterization and was therefore not considered further.

We compared the models primarily at the level of the estimated parameters rather than on the basis of information criteria, because differences in information criteria for these data are strongly affected by the treatment of responses at the scale boundaries and thus do not solely reflect differences in the operationalization of response styles. 7Estimates from the BIRM-RS and the CRM-based model corresponded closely. Person estimates of the substantive traits correlated between .84 and .90 across the two models, item difficulties between .91 and .98 within traits, and the estimated trait intercorrelations were nearly identical. ERS estimates correlated at .75, and both models indicated only weak associations between ERS and the substantive traits. Correspondence with the beta-based model of Jiang et al.

(2025) was more moderate, with correlations of .66 to .74 for the substantive traits and .63 for ERS. This model also differed from the other two in the associations it implied: ERS was moderately related to all three substantive traits (|𝑟| = .31 to .36), and the correlation between conscientiousness and narcissism was positive rather than close to zero or slightly negative. 8Overall, the BIRM-RS and the CRM-based model thus yielded convergent substantive conclusions for these data, whereas the model of Jiang et al. (2025) differed from both in several of the associations it implied.

Post-hoc Simulation

In this post-hoc simulation, we evaluated the performance of the BIRM-RS model under conditions approximating those observed in the empirical data by Kuhlmann et al. (2017).

Specifically, we specified a condition to closely match the estimated variances and covariances obtained from the empirical data. We used a sample size of 600, along with the same item structure and reverse-scoring pattern: 12 items with four reverse-scored (conscientiousness), eight items with two reverse-scored (excitement seeking), and six items without reverse-scored items (narcissism). Response style variances were set to 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐸𝑅𝑆 = 0.1 and 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝐴𝑅𝑆 = 0.15, approximating the empirical estimates, and the variances of all substantive traits were fixed to 0.5.

Correlations were specified to resemble the empirical estimates, with values of -.10 between the first and second and between the first and third traits, and .55 between the second and third traits. Correlations between ERS and the substantive traits were set to .15, -.10, and -.10, respectively. A total of 50 replications were conducted to ensure sufficient precision in the performance metrics.

Results

All models converged successfully, with 𝑅 ̂ values below 1.03. MCSEs ranged from 0.001 to 0.005. Overall, parameter recovery was good under these empirical-like conditions.

Performance measures are summarized in Figure 7. Correlations between true and estimated values exceeded .88 for most parameters, with lower values observed for the third latent trait (𝑟 = .84) and ARS (𝑟 = .85). This pattern is consistent with the low number of items for this trait and the absence of reverse-scored items.

RMSEs were similar to those observed in the main simulation study for conditions with similar numbers of items. RMSEs increased as the number of items and reverse-scored items decreased.

Regarding bias, ERS showed the largest underestimation (-0.067), consistent with the main simulation results. In contrast, the dispersion parameter exhibited the largest overestimation (0.094). The absolute bias patterns mirrored those of the RMSEs.

Variances of the latent traits were generally underestimated, with the degree of underestimation varying depending on the number of items and reverse-scored items (𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝜃1 = 0.48; 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝜃2 = 0.45; 𝑉𝑎𝑟 𝜃3 = 0.39). The variance of ARS was overestimated (0.20), whereas the variance of ERS was slightly underestimated (0.07).

In summary, the post-hoc simulation demonstrated that the BIRM-RS model achieves accurate parameter recovery under conditions closely resembling those observed in the empirical data. Although recovery was somewhat weaker for parameters associated with constructs lacking reverse-scored items, overall performance remained strong. Notably, both ARS (𝑟 = .85) and the third latent trait (𝑟 = .84) were still recovered reasonably well even though the third scale contained no reverse-scored items. This contrasts with the markedly weaker recovery of the traits and ARS in the main simulation when none of the scales included reverse-scored items. This finding suggests that reverse-scored items measuring other constructs can partly compensate for their absence within a given scale, consistent with the trait-invariant specification of ARS. These scale is fixed by the prior rather than freely estimated. This boundary case resulted in poor convergence of the ERS parameters under the centered parameterization of the person parameters used throughout this article: 𝑅 ̂ exceeded 1.01 for the ERS standard deviation in all 50 replications (median = 1.35, 95th percentile = 1.72, maximum = 2.10) and for 97.7% of the person-specific ERS parameters (median = 1.08, 95th percentile = 1.27, maximum = 1.40). In contrast, fewer than 3% of the 𝑅 ̂ values for the substantive traits, ARS, and item parameters exceeded 1.01 (maximum = 1.06). Re-estimating the BIRM-RS on the same datasets with a noncentered parameterization resolved the convergence problems (𝑅 ̂≤ 1.005 for all ERS parameters in all replications) without changing the results reported here. 9

Model selection performed reliably in both data-generating conditions. When response styles were present, LOO preferred the BIRM-RS in all 50 replications; when they were absent, it preferred the simpler BIRM in all 50 replications. WAIC selected the same model as LOO in every case.

Discussion

In the present study, we introduced and evaluated the Beta Item Response Model with

Response Styles (BIRM-RS) for modeling responses on bounded continuous scales such as VAS. Through a comprehensive simulation study, we examined the model's ability to recover person and item parameters under varying design conditions, including different numbers of items, sample sizes, numbers of reverse-scored items, and response style variances. In addition, 9 In the non-centered parameterization, the traits and ERS parameter of each person are expressed as 𝐿𝑧 𝑖 , where 𝐿 is the Cholesky factor of Σ and 𝑧 𝑖 follows a multivariate standard normal distribution. Estimates of the traits, ARS, and item parameters were virtually identical under both parameterizations (all 𝑟 ≥ .99), and LOO and WAIC again preferred the BIRM without response styles in all 50 replications. The 𝑅 ̂ distributions for all parameter groups are reported in the supplementary materials.

we applied the model to empirical data and conducted a post-hoc simulation to evaluate its performance under empirically informed conditions.

Overall, the simulation results indicated that the BIRM-RS model achieves good parameter recovery under conditions that provide sufficient item information. In particular, the number of items per substantive trait and the number of reverse-scored items emerged as critical design factors, especially for accurately estimating ARS. Response style variance also played an important role, with higher variance facilitating better recovery of the response style parameters.

More specifically, the relative magnitude of response style variance compared to substantive trait variance was a key determinant of recoverability. Notably, our post-hoc simulation demonstrated that the model performs well even under empirically realistic conditions with relatively low response style variances, likely because substantive trait variances were similarly constrained.

The empirical application further supported the utility of the BIRM-RS. Models incorporating response styles provided better fit than models without response style parameters, indicating that accounting for systematic response tendencies can improve the modeling of VAS data. This finding is particularly relevant given that one of the included constructs lacked reverse-scored items, representing a challenging scenario for identifying ARS. Taken together, these results show how well the BIRM-RS recovers its own parameters and how it behaves when applied to empirical data.

They do not establish its performance under data generated by other model families or the performance of competing models under data generated from the BIRM-RS. In the terminology of Heinze et al. (2024), the present article thus constitutes a phase I/II contribution, whereas systematic cross-model comparisons would constitute a phase III evaluation.

From a practical perspective, the BIRM-RS model demonstrated stable estimation and reliable convergence even with relatively small sample sizes. Compared to traditional IRT models for ordinal data, which often require large samples relative to the number of parameters [e.g., a ratio of approximately 5:1 between persons and parameters; De Ayala (2022)], the BIRM-RS offers a comparatively parsimonious alternative for modeling continuous responses.

This property is particularly advantageous in applied settings where sample sizes are limited. In our simulations, reliable convergence was achieved with as few as 300 participants across all conditions.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations of the present study and the BIRM-RS model warrant further investigation. First, although the simulation study covered a range of relevant design factors, additional scenarios should be explored, including more complex covariance structures and higher-dimensional trait spaces. Sensitivity analyses of prior specifications and model assumptions would also be valuable, particularly in light of the systematic over-and underestimations observed for certain parameters (e.g., ERS variance).

Second, the model relies on specific theoretical assumptions regarding the ordering of response style processes, with ARS modeled as preceding ERS. Alternative formulations could challenge this assumption and test different process orderings. A further consideration concerns the relation between ARS and the substantive traits. In the present data, posterior correlations between ARS and the three traits were negligible, and the simulation study indicated that these correlations are recovered without systematic distortion. This need not generalize to other settings: if acquiescent responding is systematically related to substantive trait levels, ARS and the substantive traits may be difficult to separate, particularly when few reverse-scored items are available. Applications of the model should therefore inspect these correlations rather than assume independence.

Third, alternative operationalizations of response styles could be considered. For example, ERS could be modeled using approaches inspired by IRTree models, in which only the most extreme responses contribute to the ERS factor (e.g., Böckenholt, 2012; De Boeck & Partchev, 2012; Khorramdel & von Davier, 2014). For ARS, adopting an operationalization closer to that proposed by Huang (2025) could be an interesting extension within the BIRM framework. Future work could also embed the BIRM-RS within the zero-and one-inflated BIRM proposed by Molenaar et al. (2022). Our sensitivity analysis suggests that the overall pattern of results is robust to the treatment of boundary responses, whereas the scaling of the latent variances is not. An integrated specification would allow response styles and boundary inflation to be estimated jointly and would permit model comparisons on a common scale.

Beyond estimation, boundary responses also raise a conceptual issue: selecting the endpoint of a scale may itself reflect extreme or acquiescent responding rather than merely constitute a nuisance to be accommodated statistically. In the present model, such responses can only be represented through the beta density and are not assigned a separate status. An integrated specification would therefore need to link the probability of a boundary response to the response style parameters, rather than simply adding an inflation component alongside them. Until such an extension is developed, estimates from the BIRM-RS should be interpreted with particular caution in applications in which a substantial proportion of responses falls at the scale boundaries.

Fourth, the current model does not include an explicit discrimination parameter.

Although the dispersion parameter 𝜏 𝑗 may capture aspects of item discrimination, the relationship between these constructs remains to be clarified. Future research should examine whether incorporating a separate discrimination parameter (Jiang et al., 2025; Molenaar et al., 2022) improves model fit and parameter recovery.

Fifth, empirical benchmarks for model parameters are currently limited. As applications of the BIRM-RS accumulate, it will become possible to identify typical parameter ranges, particularly for response style variances. Such information will inform both model specification and the design of future simulation studies.

Finally, as additional models for analyzing response styles in bounded continuous data emerge, such as those proposed by Huang (2025) and Jiang et al. (2025), comparative studies will be essential to evaluate their relative strengths and weaknesses.

Such comparisons should consider theoretical assumptions and simulation-based foundations as well as empirical performance across diverse datasets. Beyond model comparisons, the validity of the estimated response style parameters should be examined against external criteria. Response style estimates from Likert-type data are a natural candidate, but when the same items are administered in both formats, correspondence between the two sets of estimates may partly reflect shared item content. In addition, it remains an open question whether response styles are invariant across response formats. Future studies specifically designed to address these issues would provide a stronger test of the validity of the response style parameters. Moreover, integrating the BIRM-RS with other model extensions, such as those addressing careless responding (Zhang et al., 2025), represents another promising direction for future research. As VAS become increasingly popular in experience sampling methods, the model could be extended to accommodate intensive longitudinal data by incorporating random effects.

Conclusion

The BIRM-RS provides a flexible and parsimonious framework for modeling response styles in bounded continuous data. By jointly accounting for extreme, midpoint, and acquiescent response tendencies, the model extends existing approaches and enables a more nuanced analysis of VAS responses. The results of the present study suggest that, under appropriate design conditions, the BIRM-RS yields accurate and interpretable parameter estimates. With continued methodological refinement and empirical validation, the model has the potential to become a valuable tool for improving the measurement of psychological constructs using continuous response formats such as VAS. Model Misspecification and Model Selection

To examine how the BIRM-RS behaves when response styles are absent from the data, as well as the consequences of ignoring response styles when they are present, we extended the post-hoc simulation to a 2 × 2 design. Data were generated either from the BIRM-RS or from the BIRM without response styles, and each dataset was analyzed with both models. All other datagenerating conditions followed the specification described above, with 50 replications per cell and the same simulated dataset analyzed by both estimating models within each replication.

Because both models share the beta response distribution, this design addresses misspecification with respect to response styles but not with respect to the response distribution itself.

When response styles were present but not modeled, recovery of the substantive traits deteriorated (correlations of .88, .84, and .76, compared with .92, .88, and .84 under the correctly specified model), with the largest reduction for the trait measured without reverse-scored items.

Effects on the item parameters were selective: item difficulties were essentially unaffected (𝑟 = .999), whereas the dispersion parameter was substantially biased (bias of -0.46 compared with +0.09 under correct specification). Estimated trait intercorrelations also changed, with the negative correlation between the first and third traits no longer recovered.

When response styles were absent from the data but nevertheless included in the estimating model, recovery of the substantive traits was largely unaffected (correlations of .93, .89, and .85, compared with .93, .90, and .88 under the correctly specified model). The estimated ERS variance collapsed toward zero, as expected when no ERS was present in the generating model. The estimated ARS variance did not collapse toward zero in the same way, because its

Simulation StudyTo evaluate the performance of the proposed BIRM-RS model, we conducted a simulation study aimed at assessing parameter recovery. The primary objective was to examine how accurately the model recovers the true person (and item) parameters under varying experimental conditions, including differences in sample size, number of items, and the variance of response styles. Data were generated from the BIRM-RS itself. The study therefore evaluates parameter recovery under correct model specification and, by design, does not address the model's performance when the data-generating process differs from the fitted model or its performance relative to competing approaches.The primary focus was on the person parameters, namely the substantive traits 𝜃 and the response style parameters 𝜂 ERS for extreme and midpoint response styles (ERS/MRS), and 𝜂 ARS using R (R Core Team, 2024) version 4.4.2.

Item parameters included difficulty (𝛿 𝑗 ), dispersion (𝜏 𝑗 ), and item direction (reverse-scored vs. regular). Person parameters comprised two latent traits (𝜃 𝑖1 and 𝜃 𝑖2 ) as well as the response style parameters for ERS/MRS (𝜂 𝑖 ERS ) and ARS (𝜂 𝑖 ARS ). Here, 𝑗 indexes items and 𝑖 indexes persons. We included two substantive latent traits (𝜃 1 and 𝜃 2 ) in the simulation design for several reasons: (1) to allow for the modeling of response styles across multiple traits, (2) to reflect applied settings in which multiple latent dimensions are common, metric was first computed for each replication (across persons or items) and then averaged across replications.

The evaluated metrics included mean bias, mean absolute bias, mean root mean square error (RMSE), and the mean Pearson correlation between true and estimated parameter values. 3 The correlation is standardized and indicates how well the model preserves the ordering of persons on a parameter, with higher values indicating better recovery. The RMSE and the absolute bias, in contrast, are expressed in the metric of the parameter itself, with lower values indicating smaller deviations from the true values. Because these metrics are not standardized, they increase with the dispersion of the true parameter values even when relative accuracy remains unchanged. The two types of metrics can therefore point in different directions across conditions that differ in parameter variance without being contradictory. In addition to these metrics, we examined the recovery of variances and covariances of the substantive traits and the ERS parameter by comparing the estimated multivariate variance-covariance matrix to the true matrix used in data generation.

Because the degree of posterior shrinkage differs between the two specifications, this comparison is based on the variance of 𝜃 realized across persons within each posterior draw, rather than on the variance of the posterior means reported elsewhere in this article.

The BIRM-RS and the CRM-based model were fitted to the same rescaled responses, so their information criteria are formally comparable. The CRM-based model yielded lower values (LOOIC: -19,508 vs. -18,209; WAIC: -19,799 vs. -18,498). This difference was driven entirely by the 10.82% of responses that were rescaled from the boundaries to 0.0001 and 0.9999. For the remaining responses, the BIRM-RS achieved the higher log pointwise predictive density (3,649 vs. 2,674). Posterior predictive checks with replicated responses rounded to the 101 possible values of the VAS (0 to 100; see supplementary materials) showed that neither model fully reproduced the observed frequencies of boundary responses. The CRM-based model overpredicted boundary responses (5.6% vs. 4.9% at the lower bound and 6.6% vs. 5.9% at the upper bound), whereas the BIRM-RS underpredicted them (3.4% and 4.5%, respectively) as well as the number of respondents with many boundary responses. In the interior of the scale, both models reproduced the overall response distribution similarly well. The model ofJiang et al. (2025) accommodates boundary inflation and was therefore fitted to the unrescaled responses, so its information criteria are not on a common scale with those of the other two models. Information criteria for all models are reported in the supplementary materials.
